title: The Endurance Sank. How Did All 28 Men Make It Home Alive?
description:
In October 1915, the 28 men of Shackleton's Endurance, the Weddell Sea party, left their ship and stood on the pack ice. "28" here means this party only, not the whole Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition. The ship did not sink until November, and their fight to survive had only just begun.

This episode follows a chain of changing decisions: keeping three lifeboats on the ice; crossing the sea to Elephant Island after the ice broke up; six men in the James Caird choosing to run before the westerlies to the more distant South Georgia; three of them crossing the mountains to a whaling station; three rescue attempts that could not break through the ice, until Chile's Yelcho took off the 22 men left on the island on August 30, 1916. The other arm of the expedition, the Ross Sea party, lost three men, so we do not describe "the Endurance party all survived" as zero deaths for the whole expedition.

Facts follow Ernest Shackleton's South!, published in 1919. It is a memoir written after the events and also quotes other crew members' diaries; links to the relevant chapters are listed below. The images are AI-generated cartoon illustrations that support the story; they are not historical footage or reconstructions of what anyone looked like.

ed001.text: On October 27, 1915, the pack ice crushed the Endurance.

ed002.text: Ordered off the ship, the 28 men moved the lifeboats onto the ice.

ed003.text: This ice drifts and cracks; there's no fixed road underfoot.

ed004.text: Remember these three boats. Hauled by hand, how far can they go?

ed005.text: Land in view: will the ice let them ashore?

ed006.text: Later, six men pass up nearer land for a farther island. Why?

ed008.text: Off the ship, what carried them to a place help could reach?

ed009.text: That road home began on December 5, 1914, leaving South Georgia.

ed010.text: Its job: cross the Weddell Sea, land the party on Antarctica.

ed011.text: At first, the ship still found gaps in the ice.

ed012.text: By January 19, 1915, the ice all around had closed that gap.

ed013.text: The next day, Shackleton concluded the ship was truly trapped in the ice.

ed014.text: The engine could push the ship, but not a whole field of wind-driven ice. Keep burning coal?

ed015.text: In late January they shut the boilers; coal, once gone, was gone.

ed016.text: By late February, it was a floating winter camp.

ed017.text: They still lived aboard; boats and stores had to be ready to move.

ed018.text: The ice dragged the whole ship; the rudder had no say.

ed019.text: In winter, the floes pushed and squeezed, pressing on the wooden hull's sides.

ed020.text: If the ice kept the ship clamped like a block, could it hold out till spring?

ed021.text: Nine months on, the ice hadn't let go; it pressed even harder.

ed022.text: By late October, water came in and planks split under the strain.

ed023.text: Abandoning ship that first day meant giving up crossing Antarctica.

ed024.text: Shackleton later wrote that his new task was getting his men to land.

ed025.text: Now what mattered was the boats that could carry men.

ed026.text: They camped on the floe, no soil under the tents. Could they haul the boats?

ed027.text: Aiming for land, they tried to haul the boats.

ed028.text: But each ice ridge meant stopping to lift the boats.

ed029.text: The first march didn't get far, so they waited on the ice for a way through.

ed030.text: The ship stayed in view, but they could no longer live in it.

ed031.text: Only on November 21 did the ship sink between the floes.

ed032.text: The ship was gone before the shore came; where could this slab of ice take them?

ed033.text: In December they tried again, hauling toward a likelier landing.

ed034.text: Those three boats remained, but they hauled just two: about seven and a half miles in seven days.

ed035.text: More hauling could exhaust the men, so they halted and set up Patience Camp.

ed036.text: Instead of hauling, they would wait for the ice to drift them to open water.

ed037.text: Next March, they drifted level with an islet holding old supplies.

ed038.text: But it was still some sixty miles off; broken ice blocked any walk there.

ed039.text: No channel yet for the boats to pass. When could they launch?

ed040.text: In April, the floe beneath camp started forcing an immediate decision.

ed041.text: On April 9, the floe could no longer safely hold them all.

ed042.text: Wait longer and the boats couldn't launch; that day all three put to sea.

ed043.text: In the boats, low sides met wind and waves head-on.

ed044.text: The boats stayed close, finding ways through the ice.

ed045.text: By mid-April, the boats neared Elephant Island.

ed046.text: But cliffs, reefs and surf guarded it. A beach in sight; could they land?

ed047.text: They finally landed on a narrow stony beach, once seen but out of reach.

ed048.text: But tide and surf swept that beach; no place for a lasting camp.

ed049.text: Shackleton sent Wild along the coast to scout a better spot for tents.

ed050.text: Wild found a sandspit, and the party moved camp again.

ed051.text: The whole party was ashore now; nobody left at sea.

ed052.text: No harbor here to call for help; who could take word out?

ed053.text: Shackleton weighed it: the Falklands were closer, but meant rowing upwind.

ed054.text: Remember the long route? South Georgia was far, but westerlies helped and whalers had east-coast bases.

ed055.text: They took the far route in one small boat. Could it survive that sea?

ed056.text: The carpenter reinforced the roughly 20-foot James Caird with sledge wood and canvas.

ed057.text: On April 23, Shackleton named the six who would go, himself among them.

ed058.text: The other 22, led by Wild, waited on the island for news.

ed059.text: On April 24, the James Caird pushed off; those ashore watched it shrink.

ed060.text: A day after he left, ice ringed the island again. Was the route still open?

ed061.text: The James Caird sailed east; those left behind could only keep to their beach.

ed062.text: Canvas blocked some waves, but couldn't make the boat a big ship.

ed063.text: Navigator Worsley used a sextant for position; waves wouldn't wait.

ed064.text: Slightly off course, they could miss South Georgia.

ed065.text: After ten-plus days, South Georgia's peaks rose from the sea.

ed066.text: On May 10, they reached King Haakon Bay on the west coast.

ed068.text: They reached the empty west coast; whalers were across the island. How?

ed069.text: Help lay east, over icy mountains with no roads at all.

ed070.text: On May 19, Shackleton, Worsley and Crean set off.

ed071.text: Three stayed put. Would the climbers find a ship to fetch them?

ed072.text: Without sleeping bags, they kept seeking the next slope.

ed073.text: They crossed the ridge ahead, only to find more mountains. Where were the chimneys?

ed074.text: On May 20, Stromness whaling station finally appeared beyond the mountain.

ed075.text: At the station at last, the three sought a ship; the west-coast men were next.

ed076.text: A whaler fetched the three from King Haakon Bay; all six were now safe.

ed077.text: When would those on the island see a ship that could land?

ed078.text: On May 23, the first rescue ship was already at sea.

ed079.text: Steel hull, thick ice: it had to turn back.

ed080.text: In June, a ship lent by Uruguay tried again, but ice stopped it close to Elephant Island.

ed081.text: Ship three, Emma, left in July, slowed by engine woes and headwinds.

ed082.text: Near the island she hit ice again; Shackleton's third try failed.

ed083.text: No huts on the island. What would shelter those waiting?

ed084.text: The men left behind turned the boats over as a windbreak roof.

ed085.text: They kept the camp going and kept glancing out to sea for a ship.

ed086.text: Stores ran low; they gathered limpets and seaweed and boiled seal bones.

ed087.text: At the end: about two days' seal and penguin meat. Would a ship make it?

ed088.text: Chile's government provided the Yelcho; Shackleton sailed again on August 25.

ed089.text: The Chilean ship wasn't an icebreaker. Would ice block it?

ed090.text: This time wind drove the ice apart; the ship could finally close in.

ed091.text: On the island, lookouts saw through the fog: a ship, truly coming.

ed092.text: Remember the 22 left on the island? On August 30, 1916, the Chilean rescue ship finally took them off.

ed097.text: Remember that first slab of ice? Each time a road failed, they redrew people, boats and route.

ed098.text: From floe to stony beach, from the far route to the fourth rescue ship: that was how the whole party got home.

ed099.text: Which route change could most have changed the ending?

ed100.text: To follow these turns through the sources, subscribe to the channel.
